content: Non-specific cough is defined as a non-productive cough that occurs without any identifiable respiratory disease or known cause. This condition is frequently observed in pediatric clinical practice. Children with non-specific cough are often treated with various therapies, including medications typically used for asthma. The leukotriene pathway has been implicated in the sensory (neurogenic) mechanisms that are believed to play a role in the development of chronic cough. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) in managing prolonged non-specific cough in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in several databases, including the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. The most recent searches were completed in October 2010. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized controlled trials that compared LTRA with a placebo in children diagnosed with non-specific cough. Two eligible trials were identified, both of which used montelukast as the LTRA. However, no data were available for meta-analysis. In one of the studies, it was not possible to distinguish the results of children with non-specific cough from those without. In the other study, the sample sizes were extremely small, with only five children in the montelukast group and one in the placebo group. The main findings revealed no significant differences in any of the study endpoints between the montelukast and placebo groups. The total number of participants across the studies was 256, with an additional six participants from the second study. Based on the lack of robust evidence, the authors concluded that the routine use of leukotriene receptor antagonists for treating children with non-specific cough cannot be recommended.
